claims.text: Conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries.
Internal boundaries in these lamellar colonies are prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
The untreated baseline has high strength but limited ductility because of brittle, microcrack-prone internal boundaries.
Rapid, spatially targeted laser-assisted interfacial annealing can selectively modify the internal boundaries of lamellar colonies.
Controlled laser power, scan rate, and duration can thermally modify only the interfacial regions while leaving the overall lamellar architecture unaltered.
The laser treatment leaves the alloy's bulk composition unaltered.
Localized laser heating induces beneficial complexion transitions at lamellar or colony boundaries.
The induced complexion transitions improve interfacial cohesion.
Improved interfacial cohesion reduces susceptibility to microcrack nucleation during tensile loading.
Localized laser treatment can alter colony-boundary microstructure without affecting the bulk phases.
Relative to untreated material, laser-treated material will have a lower microcrack density.
Relative to untreated material, laser-treated material will have increased room-temperature tensile strength.
Relative to untreated material, laser-treated material will have increased room-temperature tensile ductility and elongation at failure.
The intervention is effective only within a laser-processing window that modifies boundaries without compromising the lamellar structure.
The effectiveness of the intervention depends on alloy-specific thermal stability and laser spatial precision.
The proposed effect is limited to room-temperature tensile-deformation conditions.
